steps.body: A parity crystal ball: **even × anything = even**. If either factor is even, the whole product pairs up perfectly. The ONLY way to build an odd product is **odd × odd**. You can call a product's parity before multiplying a single thing.
Build the product as an array and inspect its pairs.

widget.prompt: Build a 4-by-7 array. Use the 4-square rows to see whether every square can be paired.
widget.factorFeedback: Use side lengths 4 and 7 so the array shows the even factor in every row or column.
widget.lowFeedback: The array has fewer than 28 squares. Build 4 rows of 7 or 7 rows of 4.
widget.highFeedback: The array has more than 28 squares. Build 4 rows of 7 or 7 rows of 4.
widget.successFeedback: The 28 squares pair with no leftovers. One factor is even, so the whole product is even.

predict.prompt: Without finding the exact product, will 4 × 7 be even or odd?

options.label: Even — groups of 4 can be paired
It cannot be known from the factors

predict.reveal: Four can be split into pairs with no leftovers. Seven groups of those pairs still have no leftovers, so the product is even.

steps.body: WHY does an even factor guarantee an even product?
explanationVariants: 8 groups pair into 4 pairs-of-groups — whatever's inside, the whole pile splits evenly in two.
8 × 5 = (4 + 4) × 5: two identical halves of 20 each. Anything split into two equal halves is even.

widget.prompt: Before computing, you can promise 8 × 5 will be even. Why?

options.label: An even factor makes the product even.
options.feedback: Pair the 8 groups into 4 matched pairs: the product is two identical halves — even, no matter what the groups hold.

options.label: A factor ending in 5 makes it even.
options.feedback: The 5 is the ODD one here — alone it makes odd products (like 3 × 5 = 15). The even 8 is what forces evenness.

options.label: The exact product happens to be even.
options.feedback: True — but that's checking AFTER computing. The promise comes before: an even factor guarantees it in advance.

options.label: You cannot know before multiplying.
options.feedback: It is! Any even factor pairs the whole product. No multiplication with an even factor has ever come out odd.

steps.body: Why odd × odd stays odd: odd groups of an odd size — pair up everything you can, and exactly **one loner survives**. And the rule runs backwards, too: if a product is EVEN, at least one of its factors must be even.

explanationVariants: 63 is odd, and only odd × odd makes odd — so both factors are odd. (Indeed 63 = 7 × 9, both odd.)
If either factor were even, it would pair the whole product into an even number. 63 isn't even, so no even factor exists.

widget.prompt: Two whole numbers multiply to 63 — an odd number. What do you know about the factors?

options.label: Both factors must be odd
options.feedback: Odd products only come from odd × odd. Sure enough: 63 = 7 × 9 (or 21 × 3) — odd every time.

options.label: Both factors must be even
options.feedback: Even × even is always even — it could never make 63. Even one even factor would pair the product up.

options.label: One factor is even, one is odd
options.feedback: A single even factor is enough to force an even product. 63 escaped that — so no even factor anywhere.

options.label: Nothing — parity can't run backwards
options.feedback: It runs both ways! Odd product → no even factor allowed → both factors odd. The crystal ball works in reverse.

steps.body: Odd rows have a **rhythm** — build one and listen.

widget.prompt: Put the 3s row in order, starting from 3 — then watch the parity rhythm it beats.

misorderFeedback.feedback: 12 landed before 3 — but the row climbs by 3s from its own number: 3 first, then 6, 9, 12.

widget.missFeedback: Skip count by 3: 3, 6, 9, 12 — each cell is the last plus 3.
widget.successFeedback: 3, 6, 9, 12: odd, even, odd, even — an odd row alternates forever. Even rows (like the 6s) are even ALL the way.

steps.body: Use the rhythm to catch a fact.
explanationVariants: 7 × 4 has an even factor (4), so it must be even — and it's 28.
The 7s row beats odd, even, odd, even: its 4th number lands on an even beat, 28.

widget.prompt: The 7s row alternates odd, even, odd, even… What is 7 × 4?

commonErrors.feedback: 24 is 6 × 4 — the wrong row. Stay in the 7s: 7, 14, 21, and one more hop of 7.
11 adds 7 + 4. Four groups of 7 stack higher — skip count the row: 7, 14, 21, 28.
27 is odd — but the 4th beat of an odd row is EVEN (odd, even, odd, even). Parity alone rejects 27; the answer is 21 + 7.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Hop the 7s row four times: 7, 14, 21, ? — and remember the 4th beat must be even.

steps.body: A smaller two-step score, before the game's full total.
explanationVariants: 3 points × 4 levels = 12, then add the 2-point bonus at the end: 12 + 2 = 14.
The bonus is separate from the per-level rate — multiply first (3×4=12), add second (+2=14).

widget.prompt: A game gives 3 points per level for 4 levels, plus a 2-point finish bonus. What is the total score?

commonErrors.feedback: 12 is just the level points (3×4) — don't forget the bonus at the end: 12+2=14.
20 comes from adding the bonus into the RATE first ((3+2)×4) — the bonus is a one-time add-on, applied AFTER the multiplying: 12+2=14.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Multiply points-per-level by levels first (3×4=12), then add the bonus last: 12+2=14.

steps.body: Call the parity first — then earn the number.
hints: Parity first: 5 × 7 is odd × odd. What must the level points be?
5 × 7 = 35 — odd, as promised. Now the bonus joins.
explanationVariants: Levels: 5 × 7 = 35 (odd × odd → odd ✓). Bonus: 35 + 4 = 39, still odd since odd + even = odd.
Parity audit the whole chain: odd × odd = odd, then odd + even = odd — so any even total is automatically wrong. 39 fits.

widget.prompt: A learner says 5 × 7 + 4 must be even because 4 is even. Enter the score to test and correct the claim.

commonErrors.feedback: 35 is the levels only — the parity was right (odd × odd), but the 4-point bonus still joins.
31 SUBTRACTS the bonus. A bonus is points arriving, not leaving — add the 4.
40 is even — impossible! Odd × odd made 35 (odd), and odd + even stays odd. The parity crystal ball rejects 40 before any recount.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Two steps: 5 × 7 for the levels (call its parity first!), then add the even bonus — the total must stay odd.

steps.body: You can see a product's parity before it exists.
takeaways: Any even factor forces an even product; only odd × odd makes odd.
The rule reverses: an odd product proves both factors were odd.
Odd rows beat odd-even-odd-even; even rows are even throughout.
steps.teaser: one hunt left — multiples paint stripes and staircases across the hundred chart.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Look for an **even factor**. Even means pair-able — and pair-able groups pair up the WHOLE product. 2 × 9: the 2 makes two matching 9s, a perfect pair, so the product (18) is even. No even factor anywhere? Then, and only then, the product is odd.

explanationVariants: Two identical groups of 9 are a perfect pair — even by construction.

options.label: Even
options.feedback: The 2 is even — it pairs the whole product. (It's 18.)

options.label: Odd
options.feedback: The 9 is odd, but one even factor outvotes it — even × odd always lands even.

options.label: Can't tell without multiplying
options.feedback: You can tell: spot an even factor and the product is even, guaranteed. Only odd × odd ever stays odd.
